title: Joshua 19:10–16
context: The third lot falls to Zebulun, whose territory is traced by a border line running west and east from Sarid and by a short list of towns. Border descriptions like this mark out a real inheritance for each family within the tribe, though many of the places named are uncertain today. The Bethlehem named here is generally understood to be a different town from Bethlehem in Judah. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the passage as shared ground about God’s faithfulness in giving each tribe its place. Later Scripture remembers this northern region, with Naphtali, as the land where light would dawn, a hope Matthew sees fulfilled in Jesus’ ministry (Isaiah 9:1–2; Matthew 4:13–16).

verses.text: The third lot came up for the children of Zebulun according to their families. The border of their inheritance was to Sarid.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Zebulun’s lot comes up third and that its border begins at Sarid. Each tribe’s inheritance is marked out clearly, so that families know where they belong.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the lot as the means by which God himself assigned Zebulun’s place (compare Numbers 26:55–56). Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the orderly fulfillment of God’s promise.

verses.text: Their border went up westward, even to Maralah, and reached to Dabbesheth. It reached to the brook that is before Jokneam.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the westward line toward Maralah and Dabbesheth as defining the edge of Zebulun’s inheritance. Boundaries help a people live in peace with their neighbors.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the precise border as reflecting God’s careful ordering of his gift. The exact locations are uncertain, and readers in both traditions commonly focus on the meaning of the boundary rather than its precise path.

verses.text: It turned from Sarid eastward toward the sunrise to the border of Chisloth Tabor. It went out to Daberath, and went up to Japhia.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the line turning eastward toward the sunrise and reaching the border of Chisloth Tabor. The description traces the land as if walking it, a reminder that the inheritance was real ground.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the detailed border as testimony to God’s faithfulness in fulfilling promises with concrete specificity. Both traditions commonly read such descriptions as honoring the reality of God’s gift.

verses.text: From there it passed along eastward to Gath Hepher, to Ethkazin; and it went out at Rimmon which stretches to Neah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers notice Gath Hepher, later named as the hometown of the prophet Jonah (2 Kings 14:25). The towns of the allotment become places from which God raises up his servants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence connecting the allotment of land with later stories of his work. Readers in both traditions commonly find encouragement in seeing how ordinary places become part of God’s purposes.

verses.text: The border turned around it on the north to Hannathon; and it ended at the valley of Iphtah El;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the border turning north to Hannathon and ending at the valley of Iphtah El. The inheritance has a clear limit, defining where Zebulun’s responsibility lay.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the completed border as marking the fullness of God’s gift to the tribe. Both traditions commonly read the verse as concluding the boundary description without drawing doctrinal conclusions from it.

verses.text: Kattath, Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah, and Bethlehem: twelve cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the Bethlehem listed here is generally understood to be a town in Zebulun, distinct from Bethlehem in Judah. The total of twelve cities is given, though the names listed do not obviously add up to that number.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the difficulty of matching the stated total to the names given, a feature interpreters explain in more than one way. Readers in both traditions commonly hold such details with humility while affirming the reality of the inheritance.

verses.text: This is the inheritance of the children of Zebulun according to their families, these cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the closing summary as confirming that these cities and villages belong to Zebulun according to their families. Each household could know its place in God’s land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the formula as affirming the completeness of God’s allotment. Both traditions commonly connect Zebulun’s region with the later hope that light would dawn in Galilee (Isaiah 9:1–2; Matthew 4:15–16).
